evidence.title: The Impact of Race, Ethnicity, and Sex on Fairness in Artificial Intelligence for Glaucoma Prediction Models
evidence.effect: Training/external demographics differed: White 65.6% vs. 16.1% vs. 46.0%; Black 20.7% vs. 76.3% vs. 8.7%; Hispanic 4.26% vs. 2.3% vs. 12.0%.
evidence.quote: For example, there is a substantial demographic shift in regards to White (65.6% vs. 16.1% vs. 46.0%), Black (20.7% vs. 76.3% vs. 8.7%), and Hispanic (4.26% vs. 2.3% vs. 12.0%) patients between the training set, external site #1, and external site #2, respectively.

commentary.bottom_line: Sixteen sources endorse documenting dataset demographics and comparing them with served populations, but no study has tested whether doing so improves model performance or patient outcomes. One offline glaucoma benchmark shows that training and external validation populations can differ sharply by race and ethnicity.

perspectives.view: No study evaluates the practice itself. The single supplied study documents the hazard in an offline benchmark of 39,090 patients and does not measure whether documenting or comparing demographics changes decisions or outcomes. Under GRADE conventions, the endorsements reflect expert consensus rather than tested effect, so certainty about benefit cannot be rated above no direct evidence.

In the glaucoma benchmark, Black patients made up 20.7% of training data, 76.3% of one external set, and 8.7% of another, and Hispanic patients ranged from 2.3% to 12.0%. Gaps of this size suggest that a model can be validated on populations quite unlike a given local service area, which may matter most for minority-serving systems.

The benchmark shows that demographic mismatch between development and deployment sites exists, which is a precondition for performance loss in underrepresented groups. Whether recording these gaps leads staff to catch degraded performance before it reaches patients has not been tested, so the safeguard's error-catching value remains an assumption.

The FDA draft guidance on AI-enabled device software asks sponsors to describe demographic characteristics of training and validation data alongside those of the intended-use population. This creates a documentation expectation for cleared devices, but the guidance is a draft and does not by itself require health systems to compare vendor data with their own patients.

commentary.research_gap: No study tests whether documenting dataset demographics and comparing them with local populations changes procurement choices, triggers local validation, or reduces subgroup performance gaps; prospective or comparative implementation studies across health systems are needed, including measures of staff time and the thresholds used to define a significant gap.
commentary.underserved_note: No study tested the practice in any population, so no test included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy patients. The one hazard study focused on racial and ethnic minority patients and did not report insurance, language, or literacy, which suggests that demographic documentation may omit the variables most relevant to safety-net populations unless systems add them deliberately.
